title: Ethical Decision-Making: Name the Conflict, Stakeholders, Duties, and Least Harmful Path
bottomLine: Ethical problems are not solved by naming autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence or justice and stopping. Define the clinical facts, patient values/capacity, stakeholders, legal duties, equity implications and feasible options, then choose and document the most defensible patient-centred plan with consultation when conflict persists.
recognize: Ethical conflict commonly appears when values, resource limits, safety, substitute decision-making or clinician moral concerns pull in different directions.
Law, ethics and policy overlap but are not identical.
differentiate: A capable patient's informed refusal is not automatically unethical simply because it increases medical risk.
Conscientious objection does not permit patient abandonment or obstruction of legally available care; follow the applicable regulator's expectations.
assessment: Clarify capacity, goals, cultural context, power imbalance, harms/benefits, urgency, alternatives and whose interests are being prioritized.
workup: Use ethics consultation, legal/regulatory resources or Indigenous/cultural supports when complexity warrants them.
management: Use transparent shared decision-making, mitigate inequitable barriers and document the reasoning and unresolved uncertainty.
medicationSafety: Do not use sedation/restraint or medication primarily to resolve staff inconvenience or value conflict when safer alternatives exist.
redFlags: Substitute decision-maker acting contrary to applicable legal/ethical standards
counselling: Acknowledge disagreement respectfully and explain the ethical/legal limits of available options.
followUp: Revisit decisions when facts, capacity or patient goals change.
examTrap: Choosing the clinician's preferred outcome and labelling it beneficence without addressing a capable patient's values and refusal.
oneLinePearl: Ethics is structured reasoning about competing duties, not a vocabulary quiz.

title: Cultural Safety: Make the Patient's Experience of Care the Test
bottomLine: For Canadian NP practice, cultural safety goes beyond memorizing traits of cultural groups. Examine power, racism/colonialism, communication barriers and institutional practices, ask what matters to the individual, and adapt care so the patient experiences respect, choice and safety.
recognize: Cultural humility means ongoing self-reflection and avoiding assumptions about beliefs, family roles or treatment preferences.
Indigenous cultural safety requires awareness of colonial harms, anti-Indigenous racism and the need for patient-defined respectful care.
differentiate: Cultural safety is not achieved by stereotyping a patient from ancestry, language or religion.
Professional interpretation is different from asking a child/family member to translate sensitive medical information.
assessment: Ask preferred language, decision-making supports, cultural/spiritual practices relevant to care, prior harmful healthcare experiences and access barriers.
workup: Use professional interpreters, Indigenous patient navigators/Elders or cultural supports when the patient wants them and local resources permit.
management: Offer clinically safe choices, explain reasons transparently and address discriminatory/system barriers rather than blaming adherence.
medicationSafety: Ask about traditional medicines/supplements respectfully and assess interactions without dismissing cultural practices.
redFlags: Interpreter need ignored for high-stakes consent
Patient avoiding care due to prior healthcare harm
counselling: Use curiosity and permission-based questions rather than assumptions.
followUp: Check whether the care plan was feasible and felt respectful/safe to the patient.
examTrap: Choosing a treatment plan based on a presumed cultural belief rather than asking the individual patient what matters to them.
oneLinePearl: Cultural safety is judged by the patient's experience, not the clinician's intention.

title: Health Equity and Social Determinants: Treat the Barrier as Clinical Data
bottomLine: Income, housing, food security, racism, disability access, language, transportation, geography and other social/structural determinants change health outcomes and the feasibility of a treatment plan. Assess barriers without stigma and modify care so the plan can actually be carried out.
recognize: A medically ideal plan can fail when medication cost, housing instability, transportation or caregiving demands make it inaccessible.
Health inequities are shaped by structural conditions, not simply individual choices.
differentiate: Equity means allocating support according to need/barrier, not giving every patient identical resources.
Screening for social needs without a response/referral pathway can create burden without benefit.
assessment: Ask permission to discuss medication cost, food/housing, transportation, caregiving, disability accommodations, discrimination, safety and access to follow-up.
workup: Use local benefits, social work, Indigenous/community, disability and language resources when relevant.
management: Choose affordable/equivalent treatments when possible, simplify regimens, coordinate services and advocate for accessible follow-up.
medicationSafety: Food insecurity, unstable housing, heat/cold exposure and inability to store/refrigerate medication can create direct medication risk.
counselling: Use nonjudgmental language and avoid framing structural barriers as noncompliance.
followUp: Reassess whether referrals/resources were actually accessible and whether barriers changed.
examTrap: Repeating adherence teaching when the patient cannot afford or safely store the medication.
oneLinePearl: A barrier that prevents treatment is part of the clinical problem.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada health equity and determinants-of-health resources

title: Interprofessional Collaboration: Clarify Roles, Share the Plan, Close the Loop
bottomLine: Team care is safe when roles, decision ownership and follow-up are explicit. Communicate the clinical question and urgency, respect discipline-specific expertise, resolve disagreement around patient safety and confirm who is responsible for pending results/referrals rather than assuming 'the team' will handle it.
recognize: Complex patients often require pharmacy, nursing, medicine, rehabilitation, social work, dietetics and specialty collaboration.
Transitions are high-risk when responsibilities are implicit.
differentiate: Consultation does not transfer all responsibility unless care is explicitly accepted/handed over.
Hierarchy should not prevent escalation of a serious patient-safety concern.
assessment: Identify the patient's goals, disciplines needed, decision owner, pending work and barriers to communication.
workup: Use structured communication and shared documentation; escalate unresolved safety concerns through organizational pathways.
management: Create one coherent plan, reconcile conflicting recommendations and confirm the patient understands who to contact.
medicationSafety: Medication reconciliation and pharmacist collaboration are especially valuable during transitions/polypharmacy/high-risk prescribing.
redFlags: Critical result assumed to belong to someone else
Unsafe discharge because referral not accepted
counselling: Tell the patient who is coordinating which part of care and how to reach the team if the plan fails.
followUp: Confirm referrals/consults were received and recommendations integrated.
examTrap: Documenting 'referred' and assuming responsibility ended even though no clinician accepted the referral.
oneLinePearl: Collaboration works when ownership is explicit and loops are closed.

title: Clinical Leadership: Create Conditions for Safe Care, Not Just Give Instructions
bottomLine: NP leadership includes situational awareness, prioritization, communication, conflict resolution, role clarity, mentoring and systems improvement. Leadership is not positional authority alone; it is the ability to identify risk and organize people/resources so patients receive safe, equitable care.
recognize: High-risk systems failures often appear as repeated workarounds, ambiguous responsibility, communication gaps or resource inequity.
Psychological safety supports staff speaking up about risk.
differentiate: Delegation/assignment does not eliminate accountability for appropriate supervision and follow-up.
Leadership is not overriding other disciplines; it includes using their expertise effectively.
assessment: Identify the patient-safety problem, stakeholders, resources, authority, competing priorities and people affected by change.
workup: Use incident/quality data and frontline input before designing interventions.
management: Prioritize urgent harm, communicate goals/roles, remove barriers, monitor outcomes and adjust the system rather than blaming individuals for predictable failures.
medicationSafety: Medication-safety leadership includes standardized reconciliation, high-alert safeguards and response to recurring prescribing/dispensing errors.
redFlags: Known unsafe system with no mitigation
Resource allocation that predictably excludes a high-risk group
counselling: Include patients/families in relevant safety/improvement conversations and explain changes transparently.
followUp: Measure whether the intervention reduced harm and created unintended consequences.
examTrap: Responding to a recurring systems error only by retraining the individual who made the last mistake.
oneLinePearl: Leadership fixes the conditions that shape care, not just the last person's behaviour.

title: Quality and Safety Improvement: Define the Problem, Measure It, Test Change, Sustain What Works
bottomLine: Quality improvement starts with a defined local process/problem and measurable baseline. Choose an intervention linked to the cause, test it in a controlled way, monitor balancing measures and sustain/scale only when the data show meaningful improvement without creating new harm.
recognize: Process, outcome and balancing measures answer different quality questions.
A change can improve one metric while worsening workload, equity or another safety outcome.
differentiate: QI aims to improve a local system; research aims to produce generalizable knowledge, though governance boundaries can overlap.
Audit without feedback/action is measurement, not full improvement.
assessment: Define population, process, defect, baseline performance, root causes and equity implications.
workup: Use run/control charts, audits, incident reports and qualitative frontline/patient input appropriate to the problem.
management: Use small tests of change, standardize effective interventions and create ownership for ongoing monitoring.
medicationSafety: Medication-related QI should include high-alert events, reconciliation reliability and adverse-drug-event signals.
counselling: Engage patients/families when their experience or behaviour is affected by the redesigned process.
followUp: Monitor durability and balancing measures after implementation.
examTrap: Declaring a QI intervention successful because one post-change data point improved.
oneLinePearl: QI is measurable iterative change, not a one-time policy memo.

title: Evidence-Based Practice: Combine Best Evidence, Clinical Expertise, and Patient Context
bottomLine: Evidence-based practice is not blindly following the newest paper. Frame a focused question, find the best current evidence, appraise validity/applicability, integrate patient values/comorbidity/resources and monitor the real-world outcome.
recognize: Randomized trials, observational studies, diagnostic studies, systematic reviews and qualitative research answer different questions.
Statistical significance does not automatically equal clinically meaningful benefit.
differentiate: Relative risk reduction can exaggerate perceived benefit when baseline risk is low; absolute effects and harms matter.
Guideline recommendations vary in evidence certainty and strength.
assessment: Define population, intervention/exposure, comparator and outcome plus the patient's baseline risk and priorities.
workup: Prefer high-quality systematic/current sources and examine bias, confidence intervals, applicability and conflicts of interest.
management: Use evidence proportionate to certainty and patient context; choose shared decision-making when benefits/harms are preference-sensitive.
medicationSafety: Do not generalize medication benefits to excluded populations or ignore adverse-event evidence and interactions.
redFlags: Surrogate outcome used as proof of patient benefit
Evidence applied to a population not studied
counselling: Communicate uncertainty and absolute benefits/harms in understandable terms.
followUp: Update practice when stronger evidence/guidelines emerge and monitor patient outcomes after implementation.
examTrap: Choosing an intervention because one statistically significant study exists without judging bias, applicability or absolute benefit.
oneLinePearl: Evidence informs care; context and patient values determine how it is used.

title: Clinical Practice Guidelines: Use the Recommendation, Grade, Scope, and Date
bottomLine: A guideline is useful only if it is current, trustworthy and applicable to the patient/jurisdiction. Check who produced it, evidence/recommendation strength, target population, exclusions, update date and implementation context; Canadian guidance should take priority when jurisdiction matters.
recognize: Strong recommendations can exist with varying evidence certainty and may depend on values/resources.
High-change topics such as infectious disease, immunization, prescribing and screening require date-sensitive review.
differentiate: A society statement, consensus opinion and formal evidence-graded guideline are not equivalent.
A US guideline can inform science but cannot automatically replace Canadian law, funded programs, units or regulatory practice.
assessment: Confirm the patient's population/risk group and whether exclusions/comorbidities make the recommendation less applicable.
workup: Check guideline currency, methodology/conflicts and Canadian/provincial implementation before applying a threshold or schedule.
management: Individualize recommendations through shared decision-making and document justified deviation when the patient's context requires it.
medicationSafety: Drug recommendations must also be reconciled with current Canadian monographs, contraindications and formulary/access context.
redFlags: Foreign legal/regulatory rule treated as Canadian
Guideline conflicts with a time-critical patient-specific contraindication
counselling: Explain when more than one reasonable guideline-based option exists and why patient preference matters.
followUp: Refresh high-change guidance and update local pathways when recommendations materially change.
examTrap: Choosing an old memorized guideline threshold after the Canadian recommendation has changed.
oneLinePearl: Guidelines need four checks: source, strength, scope and date.
